opus-5.5.text:
I think a gap of around ten points is actually quite informative, and it's not that surprising. The public evaluation set has been out there for a long time. People have been iterating against it, looking at the tasks, tuning their prompts, their DSLs, their sampling strategies, their hyperparameters. Even if nobody is intentionally cheating, there's a kind of slow information leakage that happens whenever you repeatedly evaluate against the same fixed set and keep the things that work. You end up overfitting to the specific distribution of puzzles in that set, sometimes in ways that are very hard to notice from the inside.

There's also a second factor, which is that large language models have very likely seen discussions of the public tasks, or even the tasks themselves, in their training data, because they've been on GitHub and discussed online for years. So when an LLM-based approach is run on public tasks, part of what you're measuring may be some degree of memorization or familiarity rather than genuine on-the-fly adaptation. The semi-private set doesn't have that problem to the same extent, so it gives you a cleaner read on how much real generalization the system is doing.

So my interpretation is that the semi-private number is the one you should trust more. The public score is an upper bound, sort of an optimistic estimate. The drop tells you roughly how much of the performance was coming from familiarity with the particular tasks rather than from the ability to handle genuine novelty. And that's exactly why we keep a private and semi-private set in the first place: the whole point of ARC is to measure the ability to deal with problems you have not seen before, and you can only do that if the problems truly haven't been seen before, by the developer or by the model.

I'd add that a ten-point gap is not a disaster. It doesn't mean the approach is worthless. It's still making real progress. It just means we should be careful with headline numbers on the public set, and the field should get used to reporting on held-out data as the primary metric.

r001.rationale: The response says repeated tuning against the fixed public set leads to overfitting and interprets the semi-private score drop as reflecting familiarity with those tasks.

r002.rationale: The response does not say program-synthesis-based solutions scored equally on both sets; it describes an approximately ten-point gap.

fable-5.1.text:
I think that gap is actually one of the most informative numbers to come out of the whole exercise, because it tells you something about what the system actually learned versus what it memorized.

So the setup is that we have a public evaluation set that anyone can download, and then a semi-private set that we hold back and only run on the Kaggle side. The two sets are drawn from the same distribution, they're calibrated to be of roughly the same difficulty. A human doing these tasks would score basically the same on both. So in principle, if your system is doing genuine abstraction and reasoning, you should see roughly the same number on both sets, maybe within a couple of points of noise.

When you see a 10-point drop, that's a signal of overfitting. And it's not necessarily overfitting in the naive sense, where someone trained directly on the test set. It's more subtle than that. The public evaluation tasks have been out there for years. People have built solutions that are tuned, sometimes explicitly, sometimes just through iterative development, to the specific kinds of transformations that appear in those tasks. If you're using an LLM, there's a decent chance the public tasks or discussions of them are in the pretraining data. If you're doing program synthesis with a hand-crafted DSL, the primitives in your DSL were probably chosen by looking at the public tasks. All of that leaks information from the public set into the system, and that inflates the public score.

So my interpretation is that the semi-private number is the real number. That's the one that reflects the system's actual generalization capability. The public number is an upper bound that includes some amount of contamination, and the size of the gap is a rough measure of how much contamination there is.

I'd also say, this is exactly why we structured the benchmark this way. Without the private set, you'd have no way to detect this. You'd see the public score, you'd think the problem is more solved than it is, and you'd be measuring the wrong thing. The whole point of ARC is to measure the ability to adapt to novelty, and you can't measure that if the test isn't novel to the system.

And to be fair to the people who built these solutions, I don't think most of them did anything wrong. It's just very hard, when you're iterating on a fixed set of tasks for months, not to end up fitting to that set. That's the natural dynamic of benchmark optimization. It's why I keep saying that the gap is the interesting thing to look at, more than the absolute numbers. A system that scores 30 on public and 30 on private is, to me, more impressive than one that scores 45 and 35.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly interprets the 10-point drop as a signal of overfitting to the public tasks and says the public score is inflated by that fit.

r002.rationale: The response does not say program-synthesis solutions scored equally; it describes a 10-point gap and says hand-crafted DSLs may be tuned to public tasks.

astra-6.text:
I would interpret that gap as evidence of some overfitting to the public set. And that doesn’t necessarily mean someone explicitly trained on the evaluation examples. When a benchmark is public, you can make design choices, select techniques, and tune your system based on what works there. Over time, the public set becomes part of your development process.

The semi-private set is meant to test the same kind of capabilities, so a drop of about ten percentage points suggests that some of the public performance doesn’t generalize. That doesn’t invalidate the solution or mean it hasn’t made progress. But I would put more weight on its performance on tasks that weren’t available during development. With ARC, the question is whether you can adapt to a genuinely new task, rather than how well you’ve adapted your system to the benchmark.

r001.rationale: It says the roughly ten-point gap is evidence of overfitting to the public set.

r002.rationale: It describes a performance drop on the semi-private set and does not state that program-synthesis-based solutions scored equally on both sets.

sol-6.1.text:
I would interpret that as evidence of some degree of overfitting to the public set. The public tasks are available for people to inspect, so even if you’re not explicitly training on them, your choices about the system—what approaches you try, what components you keep—are informed by those tasks. You can overfit through the development process itself.

The semi-private set gives you a better indication of how well those choices generalize to unseen tasks. A ten-percentage-point drop doesn’t mean the approach has no value, but it does suggest that the public score overstates its generalization performance. You would also want to look at the uncertainty around those scores before drawing a stronger conclusion.

r001.rationale: The response says the roughly ten-point drop suggests overfitting to the public set and that the public score overstates generalization.

r002.rationale: The response does not say program-synthesis-based solutions scored equally; it describes a ten-point decline on the semi-private set.
